newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK FINMIN SLAMMED OVER T-BILL AUCTION MESS.
newsitem.headline: GREEK FINMIN SLAMMED OVER T-BILL AUCTION MESS.

text.p: A late decision by the Greek finance ministry to notify banks that they would be entitled to a selling commission of 0.45 percent shortly before the closing of Monday's T-bill auction was blasted by many banks which called it unfair.

"All banks did not have the same time at their disposal to market the T-bills to their clients because they did not receive the information at the same time," said a senior foreign bank dealer. "This is an unfair practice."
Many dealers said the unequal distribution of information among banks and other investors would hurt the finance ministry's efforts to cut its cost of borrowing and lower its public debt.

"The finance ministry would be the big loser at the end," said a bond dealer at another foreign bank. "They (ministry) should understand that we cannot call foreign investors and ask them for new prices telling them that the auction opened again. This is unheard of."

Greece auctioned 300 billion drachmas of 12-month T-bills today. The average accepted price stood at 90.15 and the cuttoff price at 90.04. Another 90 billion drachmas of 12-month T-bills were allocated in non-competitive bids.
Monday's was the second competitive price auction of 12-month T-bills in the last few years.

Commercial banks used to get a commission of 0.45 percent for selling T-bills to their customers in the past but the general market impression was that no commission would be paid to banks for this auction.
"We were informed of the finance ministry's decision upon submitting the sealed envelop and we were given extra time to change our bids," said a dealer at a foreign bank.
The terms of the auction specified that all bids should have been submitted by 1200 local (1000GMT). Sources told Reuters that at least two banks submitted bids after the formal deadline.

Asked if this constituted a change in the terms of the auction, a central bank official told Reuters that this was not the case because no sealed envelope was opened before all banks submitted final bids.
But some dealers said the terms of the auction had been clearly violated.

Other sources told Reuters that the finance ministry changed its mind after being informed that the average yield at the auction would likely be much higher than 10.90 percent because banks would get no commission.

"This is Balkans. What else can I tell you," said a furious dealer for what he called lack of preparation and sloppiness on the part of the finance ministry. "You get international credit agencies upgrading you and then you have this."
Moody's recently upgraded Greek domestic debt paper to A2 even though Greece failed to submit a written request. Greek domestic securities had never been rated before.
"If I did such a gaffe I would lose my job," said another dealer. "But these guys do not have to worry about it. They are civil servants and they can go on ridiculing us and get away with it."
All dealers agreed that the finance ministry should take steps so that similar episodes not be repeated in the future.
"I hope it is the last time we see this sloppiness and unequal diffusion of information but I doubt it," he said. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
